title: Spatially dispersive photogalvanic effects as a probe of quantum geometric tensor
authors: Yicong Chen, Bumseop Kim, Senin Ahammed Akkara Paramban, Zhurun Ji, Utkarsh Khandelwal, Shupeng Xu, Jiachen Shi, Sergiy Krylyuk, Albert V. Davydov, Andrew M. Rappe, Ritesh Agarwal
abstract: Berry curvature and quantum metric of Bloch states govern a wide range of phenomena, yet unified experimental access to both remains limited. Here we show that light spatial-dispersion alters the selection rules of second-order photocurrents and responses forbidden by parity become allowed in centrosymmetric crystals without any external fields, magnetic order, interfaces, strain, or engineered symmetry breaking. The resulting response is intrinsic and its weight is set by the quantum geometry of the Bloch states. Conventional photogalvanic effects are constrained by crystal symmetry and entangle the quantum metric with shift vector contributions. The spatially-dispersive response instead isolates the quantum metric and Berry curvature in distinct polarization channels. Implementing this approach in 1T'-MoTe2 across its temperature-driven transition to Td-Weyl phase, we resolve helicity-even and helicity-odd photocurrents corresponding to quantum metric and Berry curvature contributions, respectively, from the same device. The metric-dominated response persists across both phases and exhibits a robust spectral structure reproduced by first-principles calculations and linked to momentum-resolved quantum metric hotspots. In contrast, the curvature-driven channel emerges only when inversion symmetry is broken and shows strong sensitivity to carrier doping through competing momentum-space contributions. Our results establish photogalvanic effects with spatially varying optical fields as a general route to accessing quantum geometry in materials where photon energy and electronic filling probe different parts of the excitation manifold.
summary: This paper introduces the use of spatially dispersive photogalvanic effects as a novel technique to experimentally separate and quantify the quantum metric and Berry curvature components of the quantum geometric tensor. Using $	ext{MoTe}_2$, the authors demonstrate that the linear and circular components of the photocurrent correspond, respectively, to these two geometric quantities. This method proves highly valuable for characterizing topological properties in materials across different structural phases and doping levels.
main_problem: The study aims to develop an optical protocol to simultaneously and independently probe both the Berry curvature and the quantum metric components of the quantum geometric tensor (QGT). This overcomes limitations in conventional methods that often require external symmetry breaking or fail to separate these contributions.
main_result: The spatially dispersive photogalvanic effect successfully separates the response into helicity-even ($	ext{s-LPGE}$, metric-dominated) and helicity-odd ($	ext{s-CPGE}$, curvature-driven) channels. Furthermore, the $	ext{s-CPGE}$ response is shown to be highly sensitive to carrier doping, exhibiting a systematic spectral shift.
method: The research combines experimental measurements of polarization-dependent photocurrents using spatially focused laser beams with first-principles electronic structure calculations to model the momentum-resolved contributions.
model_or_system: The primary platform is $	ext{MoTe}_2$, a material chosen for its temperature-tunable structural transition from an inversion-symmetric $1	ext{T}'$ phase to an inversion-broken $	ext{Td}$ phase. The response is analyzed based on interband transitions governed by the material's electronic band structure.
key_observables: Polarization-dependent photocurrent components ($	ext{s-LPGE}$ and $	ext{s-CPGE}$), spectral dependence on photon energy, and the shift of characteristic spectral dips with doping.
important_parameters: Temperature (e.g., 300 K vs 77 K), doping concentration (e.g., W substitution), and the polarization angle ($\phi$) of the incident light.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the spatially dispersive current can be decomposed into distinct helicity-even and helicity-odd components, and that doping effects can be modeled by a rigid chemical-potential shift.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the polarization-dependent photocurrent measurements, showing the emergence of $	ext{s-CPGE}$ upon cooling. They also compare calculated $	ext{s-LPGE}$ and $	ext{s-CPGE}$ spectra to experiment, demonstrating the spectral evolution and the doping-induced blue shift of the $	ext{s-CPGE}$ dip.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical basis for using spatially dispersive photogalvanic effects to probe the QGT. It then presents experimental evidence using $	ext{MoTe}_2$ across a structural transition to separate metric and curvature contributions. Finally, it explores the sensitivity of the curvature-driven response to doping via theoretical modeling.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, non-invasive optical tool to map out fundamental topological invariants (Berry curvature and quantum metric) in solid-state materials, which is crucial for understanding topological electronic phases.
